choices: The checked map should be stored in a ref instead of state so it survives re-renders
Using the array index as the key makes React reuse the wrong component instances after reorder — use the stable todo id as the key
setChecked must use a functional update twice to flush the batch before the reorder
The TodoItem component needs React.memo so its checked prop does not go stale
scenarios.hint: What does the key tell React when the array order changes — and what happens to the component instance sitting at position 0?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what is the correct fix?
scenarios.situation: A todo list lets users check items off and reorder them with up/down buttons. After reordering, the wrong items appear checked.
scenarios.title: The shuffling checklist
scenarios.why: Keys tell React which component instance corresponds to which data across renders. With key={i}, after a reorder React keeps the component instance at each position and just hands it new props, so any per-instance state (or DOM state like focus) sticks to the position, not the item. A stable unique id (key={t.id}) keeps identity attached to the data.

choices: The input needs an onChange handler that updates the state, otherwise the value prop pins it read-only
The input needs defaultValue instead of value because value is reserved for forms submitted to a server
useState must be initialized with a callback so the input registers as controlled
The placeholder attribute conflicts with value — remove the placeholder
scenarios.hint: Who owns the text the user sees — the DOM, or the state? What happens on a keystroke if nothing writes back to state?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what is the minimal fix?
scenarios.situation: A search field renders with an initial value but the user cannot type into it — keystrokes do nothing and the cursor stays put.
scenarios.title: The input that won't type
scenarios.why: An input with a value prop and no onChange is a controlled component whose displayed value is locked to state. React even warns about it: 'You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler.' Adding onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} makes each keystroke flow through state back into the input.

choices: Store theme and user in module-level variables so every component can import them directly
Pass a single props object containing everything to reduce the number of named props
Use composition with children, or React context, so intermediate components no longer forward props they don't use
Convert every intermediate component to a custom hook so props flow through hook return values
scenarios.hint: Which components actually need these values — and what mechanism lets a deep component read data without every layer in between touching it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the cleanest refactor that removes the prop drilling?
scenarios.situation: A theme object and a current-user object are passed as props through five intermediate components that never use them, just to reach a deep Avatar and Toolbar.
scenarios.title: Drilling through five layers
scenarios.why: Prop drilling makes intermediate components coupled to data they don't consume. The idiomatic fixes are composition (pass the deep content as children so Layout never sees the props) or context (provide theme/user once, consume where needed). Module-level mutable variables break concurrent rendering and testability.

choices: JSX cannot render numbers inside a div — wrap count in String(count) before rendering
The && operator returns the left operand when it is falsy, so count={0} renders the number 0 — compare explicitly, e.g. {count > 0 && ...}
The badge span needs a key so React can remove it when count changes to zero
Conditional rendering requires a ternary; && is only valid for boolean props
scenarios.hint: What does the expression `0 && <span/>` evaluate to — and which of those values does JSX actually render?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the stray 0, and how should the condition be written?
scenarios.situation: A cart badge should show the item count only when there are items. With zero items, the page renders a stray '0' next to the cart icon.
scenarios.title: The phantom zero
scenarios.why: JSX renders any value except null, undefined, booleans, and empty fragments. count && <span/> evaluates to 0 when count is 0, and 0 is rendered as text. The fix is an explicit boolean condition (count > 0 && ...) or a ternary. This is the classic 'falsy render' gotcha with 0, '', and NaN.

choices: Return an array of the two <tr> elements with keys instead of any wrapper
Use a keyed Fragment — <Fragment key={row.id}> — which groups the rows without adding a DOM node
Wrap in <tbody> per row so each pair gets its own table section
Move the key onto the first <tr> and leave the wrapper keyless
scenarios.hint: You need a wrapper that satisfies React's key requirement but contributes nothing to the DOM. Which wrapper accepts a key and renders nothing itself?
scenarios.prompt: How should the mapped pairs be wrapped?
scenarios.situation: A table body maps rows into pairs of <tr> elements (a data row plus a detail row). Wrapping each pair in a div breaks the table layout, and React warns about missing keys.
scenarios.title: Two nodes where one was expected
scenarios.why: A <div> inside <tbody> is invalid HTML and breaks table layout. The shorthand <> cannot take a key, but the explicit <Fragment key={...}> can — it satisfies the list-key requirement while adding zero DOM nodes. Returning arrays with keys also works but is noisier.

choices: React.memo only works on class components; function components need useMemo instead
The inline options object and inline onSelect arrow function create new references every render, so the shallow prop comparison always fails
React.memo requires a custom comparison function as the second argument or it re-renders always
The data prop is an array, and React.memo cannot compare arrays — it must be serialized first
scenarios.hint: React.memo compares props with Object.is per prop. What is Object.is({a:1}, {a:1}) — and what does the JSX create on each render?
scenarios.prompt: What is defeating the memoization?
scenarios.situation: A heavy Chart component is wrapped in React.memo, but profiling shows it re-renders on every parent render even though its data hasn't changed.
scenarios.title: The memoized child that never memoizes
scenarios.why: React.memo does a shallow comparison of props. An object or function literal in JSX creates a brand-new reference on every parent render, so the comparison sees 'changed' props even when the contents are identical. Hoist the object outside the component (or useMemo it) and stabilize the callback with useCallback.

choices: setInterval callbacks cannot call setState — the interval must dispatch through a ref
The effect closure captures count = 0 forever, so every tick sets 0 + 1 — use the functional updater setCount(c => c + 1)
The empty dependency array prevents re-renders; add count to the dependencies
clearInterval in the cleanup runs after the first tick and stops the timer
scenarios.hint: What value of `count` does the interval callback see on its tenth tick — and when was that callback created?
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
scenarios.situation: A timer component should increment every second, but the displayed count goes 0 → 1 and then never changes again.
scenarios.title: The counter that stalls at one
scenarios.why: This is the classic stale closure: the interval callback closes over the count value from the first render (0) and the empty deps array means the effect never re-subscribes. Every tick computes 0 + 1. The functional updater form reads the latest state at call time, so setCount(c => c + 1) is correct regardless of what the closure captured.

choices: fetch is not allowed inside useEffect — data fetching must happen in event handlers
The effect has no dependency array, so it runs after every render; each setUser triggers a render, which re-runs the effect — add [userId]
setUser inside .then creates a promise cycle; the state setter must be called synchronously
userId is a prop and props change identity each render, so the effect can never stabilize
scenarios.hint: After the fetch resolves and setUser runs, what happens next — and what makes the effect run again?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the effect?
scenarios.situation: After adding a data-fetch effect, the network tab shows the same request firing hundreds of times and the page becomes unresponsive.
scenarios.title: The effect that never rests
scenarios.why: An effect with no dependency array runs after every completed render. The fetch resolves, setUser triggers a re-render, the effect runs again — an infinite fetch loop. Adding [userId] restricts re-runs to actual userId changes. (Also consider an abort/cancellation for race safety, but the loop itself is the missing deps array.)

choices: The effect must return a cleanup function that unsubscribes, otherwise every symbol change adds another live subscription that keeps firing setPrice
subscribe must be called outside the effect because effects cannot hold subscription handles
setPrice needs a functional update or the subscription delivers stale prices
The dependency array should be empty so the subscription is created only once
scenarios.hint: When `symbol` changes, the effect runs again. What happens to the subscription created by the previous run?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and why does it matter?
scenarios.situation: A component subscribes to a live price feed in an effect. Users report stale prices piling up and the tab slowing down after navigating between symbols.
scenarios.title: The leaking subscription
scenarios.why: Effects that create persistent resources — subscriptions, timers, listeners — must return a cleanup function. React runs cleanup before re-running the effect (on symbol change) and on unmount. Without it, each symbol change leaves the old subscription alive: duplicate updates, memory growth, and setState calls on unmounted components.

choices: Move the total calculation into a second useState initialized from items so they update atomically
Compute the total during render instead of storing it — const total = items.reduce(...); derivable values shouldn't be separate state
Add total to the effect's dependency array so the effect re-runs until they agree
Use useRef for the total so updates don't trigger extra renders
scenarios.hint: Can the total ever be anything other than a function of `items`? If not, what does storing it separately buy you — and what can go wrong in between?
scenarios.prompt: What is the better pattern?
scenarios.situation: A cart stores items in state and also stores the total in state, updated by an effect. Users occasionally see a total that doesn't match the items.
scenarios.title: The total that lags behind
scenarios.why: State that can be computed from other state is derived state, and syncing it with an effect creates a window where the two disagree (plus extra renders). Computing it during render guarantees it is always consistent with items. Reserve useState for values that are truly independent sources of truth.

choices: React batches the three updates and each one reads the same stale count value — use the functional form setCount(c => c + 1) three times
setState is asynchronous and only the last call in a handler is kept — spread the calls across three handlers
The button needs three separate onClick handlers, one per increment
useState cannot be called conditionally in a loop — use useReducer instead
scenarios.hint: All three calls read the same variable. What value does each one compute — and what would happen if each update were expressed as 'take the latest value and add one'?
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A button handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times, but the counter only goes up by one per click.
scenarios.title: Three increments, one bump
scenarios.why: React batches state updates within an event handler, and all three calls close over the same count from the current render — each computes count + 1 from the identical base. The functional updater queues transformations (c => c + 1) that React applies in order, so three queued updaters yield +3. (useReducer is also a fine alternative for complex updates.)

choices: useState for both — state is the only way to persist values across renders
useRef for both — a ref holds a mutable .current that persists across renders without triggering re-renders; state would cause an infinite render loop for the counter
useMemo for both — memoized values persist without re-rendering
Module-level variables — they persist across renders and never trigger updates
scenarios.hint: What happens if you call a state setter during render — and which hook gives you a mutable box that React never watches?
scenarios.prompt: Which tool fits, and why not state?
scenarios.situation: You need to track how many times a component rendered for a diagnostics panel, and also hold a reference to an input to focus it on mount — without causing extra renders.
scenarios.title: Counting renders without re-rendering
scenarios.why: useRef returns a stable object whose .current you can mutate freely; writes don't schedule renders, so incrementing a render counter in the body (or an effect) is safe. useState would re-render on every write — writing during render would loop forever. Refs are also the canonical way to reach DOM nodes. Module variables are shared across component instances and break with concurrent rendering.

choices: useParams returns all values from the URL including query strings, so it already includes the search term
URLSearchParams is only available in Node, not the browser — parse location.search manually with a regex
useParams reads path segments like :id; the search text lives in the query string, read with useSearchParams
Query strings must be stored in component state because React Router ignores everything after ?
scenarios.hint: Split the URL at the `?`. Which part is the route pattern responsible for, and which part is free-form?
scenarios.prompt: Which hook gives the component the search text?
scenarios.situation: A product page route is /products/:id. The URL also carries a search box term as ?q=headphones. The component needs both the id and the query.
scenarios.title: Path params versus the query string
scenarios.why: useParams extracts dynamic path segments defined in the route pattern (:id). Everything after ? is the query string, handled by useSearchParams, which returns a URLSearchParams-backed pair. Mixing them up is common: path params identify the resource, search params carry optional UI state like filters and sorting.

choices: Move the fetch into useEffect inside ProductPage and handle errors with a local error state
Define a loader on the route that fetches the product, read it with useLoaderData, and declare errorElement on the route to catch loader/render failures
Fetch in the loader but store the result in a context provider so useLoaderData isn't needed
Loaders can only return static JSON imports, so fetch must happen in an action instead
scenarios.hint: What React Router primitive fetches data before the route renders — and what primitive catches errors thrown during that load?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic React Router approach?
scenarios.situation: A product page should fetch its data before rendering and show a dedicated error page if the product doesn't exist or the fetch fails.
scenarios.title: Loading before the route renders
scenarios.why: React Router loaders run before the route element renders; the component reads the result with useLoaderData, and errorElement renders when the loader (or the route's render) throws. This co-locates data requirements with routes and avoids the loading-state-then-error-state dance inside every component.

choices: Set cacheTime to zero so every mount refetches, guaranteeing fresh data
Raise staleTime (e.g. to 5 minutes) so remounts within that window reuse cached data without a background refetch
Move the query into a global context so the cache is shared across pages
Set refetchOnWindowFocus to false — that is the only setting that affects remount behavior
scenarios.hint: TanStack Query distinguishes 'data exists in cache' from 'data is fresh'. Which setting controls the fresh window?
scenarios.prompt: Which setting fixes the refetch-every-visit behavior?
scenarios.situation: A users list refetches from the server every time the user navigates back to the page, even seconds later. The list rarely changes.
scenarios.title: The list that refetches on every visit
scenarios.why: TanStack Query marks cached data stale immediately by default (staleTime: 0), so any remount triggers a background refetch. Raising staleTime defines a freshness window during which cached data is served without refetching. (cacheTime/gcTime controls how long unused data is kept at all — a different concern.)

choices: Call e.persist() so the synthetic event survives the async submission
Call e.preventDefault() and read the values from the form (FormData or controlled state), then submit programmatically
Forms in React must use uncontrolled inputs or the browser blocks submission
Replace the form with divs and buttons — form elements trigger full-page reloads by design in SPAs
scenarios.hint: What does a browser do natively when a form submits — and who needs to stop it?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the submit handler?
scenarios.situation: Submitting a React signup form causes a full page reload, wiping app state, instead of the intended async POST.
scenarios.title: The form that reloads the page
scenarios.why: A native form submission navigates the browser (GET/POST to the action URL, defaulting to the current page). In an SPA you must call e.preventDefault() in onSubmit, then perform the fetch yourself. (React Router actions and the newer useActionState are alternatives, but preventDefault remains the fundamental fix.)

choices: Debounce the input so fewer requests fire — the last response always wins anyway
Track the latest request (AbortController, or an incrementing request id checked before setResults) so a slow earlier response can't overwrite newer results
Move the fetch into a layout effect so it runs before paint and responses arrive in order
Store results in a ref instead of state so out-of-order writes don't trigger renders
scenarios.hint: Two requests are in flight: one for 'reac', one for 'react'. The first one finishes last. Which setResults call runs last — and whose data does the UI show?
scenarios.prompt: What can go wrong, and what is the standard fix?
scenarios.situation: A search box fetches suggestions as the user types. Occasionally the dropdown shows results for an older query than what's in the box.
scenarios.title: The dropdown that answers the wrong question
scenarios.why: Network responses don't arrive in request order. Without cancellation, a slow response for an earlier query can land after the current one and overwrite state — the classic race condition. The standard fix is an AbortController in the effect cleanup (aborting the previous request) or ignoring responses whose request id isn't the latest.

choices: Declare the settings pages as child routes of the dashboard route and render <Outlet /> where the child should appear
Copy the sidebar JSX into every settings page so each page is self-contained
Use a context provider in the dashboard that manually switches which settings component renders
Nested routes are not supported — flatten everything into top-level routes
scenarios.hint: The child routes exist, and the layout exists. What placeholder does the layout render to say 'the matched child goes here'?
scenarios.prompt: How does the shared layout display the child page?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard has a persistent sidebar and header. Settings and billing pages should render inside that layout without remounting it.
scenarios.title: The layout that swallows its children
scenarios.why: Child routes render into the parent's <Outlet />. Without it, the layout renders but the matched child has nowhere to go — a common 'blank content area' bug. This pattern keeps the layout mounted across navigations, preserving its state (e.g., collapsed sidebar) while only the outlet region swaps.

choices: React.memo compares state, not props, so it cannot help a prop-driven component
The parent passes data as a stable module-level constant, so memo can never detect changes
The inline arrow function onSelect creates a new function reference each render, defeating the shallow prop comparison — stabilize it with useCallback
React.memo is broken by the console.log inside the callback; remove all logging from memoized components
scenarios.hint: React.memo does a shallow comparison. Which prop is a brand-new value on every render even though nothing 'changed'?
scenarios.prompt: What is defeating the memoization, and how do you fix it?
scenarios.situation: A heavy Chart component is wrapped in React.memo and its data prop is stable, but it still re-renders whenever the parent re-renders.
scenarios.title: The memoized chart that keeps redrawing
scenarios.why: An inline arrow function is a new reference every render, so memo's shallow compare always sees a 'changed' onSelect prop. Wrapping the callback in useCallback (with correct deps) gives it a stable identity. The general rule: memo only pays off when all props are referentially stable — audit inline functions and objects first.

choices: Move the computation into useEffect and store the result in state to avoid blocking the render phase
Wrap the computation in useMemo with the correct dependencies so it only recomputes when inputs change
Convert the component to a class component — class render methods are memoized by default
Split the computation across multiple components so each renders a slice faster
scenarios.hint: The input rarely changes, but the component re-renders often for other reasons. Which hook caches a computed value across renders?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right optimization?
scenarios.situation: A report component aggregates 50,000 transactions on every render, making unrelated UI interactions feel sluggish.
scenarios.title: The render that recomputes the world
scenarios.why: useMemo caches the result of an expensive computation and only recomputes when its dependencies change. Storing it in state via an effect adds an extra render and a sync hazard; the computation is derived data, so memoizing it at render time is the direct fix. (Profile first — memo has its own cost and isn't free.)

choices: Context values are deeply compared, so only changed fields trigger updates — the bug must be elsewhere
The provider creates a new object literal each render, so every consumer re-renders on any parent render — memoize the value with useMemo or split into separate contexts
Consumers must be wrapped in React.memo or context updates propagate to the whole tree
Context should be replaced with a global state library; built-in context always re-renders everything
scenarios.hint: What does `{ theme, setTheme }` create on each render — and how does React decide whether consumers need to update?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the excessive re-renders, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A theme context provider wraps the whole app. Profiling shows every consumer re-rendering whenever anything in the provider's parent re-renders, even when the theme didn't change.
scenarios.title: The context that notifies everyone
scenarios.why: Context uses reference identity: when the provider's value prop is a new object (a fresh literal each render), React notifies all consumers regardless of whether the contents changed. Memoizing the value with useMemo (deps [theme]) keeps the reference stable. Splitting into separate ThemeContext/SetThemeContext further isolates readers from updaters.

choices: Paginate the data on the server — 10,000 DOM nodes is never acceptable in any form
Use React.memo on each row so only changed rows re-render
Virtualize the list (render only the visible window, e.g. with a windowing library) so the DOM stays small regardless of data size
Store the rows in a ref instead of state so React skips reconciling them
scenarios.hint: The data is fine in memory — the cost is 10,000 real DOM nodes. What technique renders only the slice the user can see?
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard solution?
scenarios.situation: An audit log renders 10,000 rows. Scrolling janks and every interaction lags, even though each row is cheap.
scenarios.title: Ten thousand rows of lag
scenarios.why: The bottleneck is DOM size, not React diffing: 10,000 nodes means huge layout/paint costs. Windowing (virtualization) renders only the visible rows plus a small overscan buffer, keeping the DOM at a few dozen nodes while the scrollbar still reflects the full dataset. Server pagination is complementary, but virtualization fixes the client-side cost directly.

choices: Move the admin components into the main bundle and rely on HTTP/2 multiplexing to hide the cost
Wrap the admin routes with React.lazy and a Suspense boundary so that chunk loads only when the route is visited
Add the admin components to the preload list in index.html so they download in parallel
Code splitting only works with class components — convert the admin pages first
scenarios.hint: You want the admin code in a separate chunk that the browser fetches on demand. Which React API turns an import() into a component?
scenarios.prompt: How should the admin routes be loaded?
scenarios.situation: Bundle analysis shows rarely-visited admin pages adding 900 kB to the initial JavaScript bundle that every visitor downloads.
scenarios.title: The bundle everyone downloads
scenarios.why: React.lazy wraps a dynamic import() so the component becomes its own chunk, fetched only when first rendered; Suspense provides the loading fallback. Route-level splitting is the highest-leverage split: visitors who never open /admin never download admin code. (Named exports need an intermediate module re-exporting as default for lazy.)

choices: Throttle the input with a 500ms debounce so filtering runs less often
Defer the query value with useDeferredValue so the list renders with the previous query until the new filter is ready, keeping the input responsive
Move the filter into a web worker — deferred values don't apply to array filtering
Store the filtered list in a ref to skip re-renders during typing
scenarios.hint: The input must stay responsive (urgent) while the heavy filter can lag a frame or two (transition). Which hook marks a value as non-urgent?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic fix for the stuttering input?
scenarios.situation: Typing in a catalog search stutters because filtering 20,000 products runs synchronously on every keystroke.
scenarios.title: The search box that stutters
scenarios.why: useDeferredValue splits the update: the input stays on the urgent, responsive value while the expensive list re-renders against a deferred (slightly lagging) value, and React can interrupt the background render if the user keeps typing. Debouncing also helps but adds latency to every keystroke; deferred values keep the UI feeling instant.

choices: Queries that match by CSS class, since classes are the most stable hook in the markup
Role-based queries (getByRole) that mirror how users and assistive tech find elements
Direct DOM traversal with container.querySelector to avoid Testing Library abstractions
Snapshot tests of the full rendered HTML, which catch every change at once
evidence:
// TODO: assert the submit button is disabled until the form is valid
render(<LoginForm />);
scenarios.hint: If a sighted user and a screen reader both need to find the button, what selector sees the page the way they do?
scenarios.prompt: Which query strategy should the test use?
scenarios.situation: A login form test needs to assert the submit button is disabled until the form is valid. The team debates how to select the button.
scenarios.title: How should the test find the button?
scenarios.why: Testing Library's guiding principle is to test the way users experience the UI. getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }) finds the button through its accessible role and name — the same path assistive technology uses — and it breaks if the button becomes unreachable, which is exactly what you want a test to catch. Test IDs and class selectors test implementation details.

choices: fireEvent is deprecated and must be replaced by dispatchEvent in all tests
userEvent dispatches the full sequence of browser events (pointerdown, focus, input, change) like a real user, catching bugs fireEvent misses

Bugs involving focus, selection, or multi-event handlers only surface under the realistic sequence. (userEvent APIs are async and must be awaited.)

choices: Wrap the assertion in waitFor (or findBy*) so the test retries until the async fetch resolves and the UI updates

scenarios.why: The first render shows a loading state; the name appears only after the promise resolves. waitFor (or the findBy* queries, which wrap it) retries the assertion until it passes or times out, matching the async reality. Fixed sleeps are flaky and slow; asserting on mocks instead of UI tests the wrong thing.

scenarios.why: Mock at the network seam — stub global fetch or the API client module — and let the component's real logic (loading states, mapping, error handling) execute against canned responses. scenarios.why: Tests coupled to implementation (state variables, handler names, internal structure) break on every refactor and discourage improvement. choices: Add a try/catch around the render method — errors in render are caught like any exception
Wrap the risky subtree in an error boundary: a class component implementing getDerivedStateFromError / componentDidCatch (or a library equivalent)

scenarios.hint: Which React mechanism catches errors thrown during rendering — and what kind of component implements it?
scenarios.prompt: How should the crash be contained?
scenarios.situation: A widget throws when it receives malformed data, unmounting the entire dashboard instead of just the widget.
scenarios.title: One bad widget takes down the page
scenarios.why: An uncaught render error unmounts the whole React tree. choices: Disable SSR for the page — hydration is incompatible with dynamic content
Make the server and client output deterministic (e.g., render the timestamp only after mount via useEffect/useState)
Add suppressHydrationWarning to every dynamic element as a general policy
Hydration mismatches are harmless warnings; the client silently fixes the DOM
scenarios.hint: The server renders at request time; the client hydrates a moment later. What value differs between those two moments?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the mismatch, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A server-rendered clock shows a hydration mismatch warning: server HTML and the first client render disagree.

Split node_modules into a separate chunk — vendors chunk always loads faster

lessons.title: Components & JSX — Core concepts
concepts: Keys tell React which component instance corresponds to which data across renders. Returning arrays with keys also works but is noisier.

Controlled components: prop drilling makes intermediate components coupled to data they don't consume. An input with a value prop and no onChange is a controlled component whose displayed value is locked to state.

Form inputs: react even warns about it: 'You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler.' Adding onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} makes each keystroke flow through state back into the input.
Composition: the idiomatic fixes are composition (pass the deep content as children so Layout never sees the props) or context (provide theme/user once, consume where needed).

pitfalls: Common trap: react.memo only works on class components; function components need useMemo instead.

lessons.title: State & Effects — Core concepts
concepts: Functional updates: the functional updater form reads the latest state at call time, so setCount(c => c + 1) is correct regardless of what the closure captured. React batches state updates within an event handler, and all three calls close over the same count from the current render — each computes count + 1 from the identical base.
Closures in effects: effects that create persistent resources — subscriptions, timers, listeners — must return a cleanup function.

Effect dependencies: state that can be computed from other state is derived state, and syncing it with an effect creates a window where the two disagree (plus extra renders). The fetch resolves, setUser triggers a re-render, the effect runs again — an infinite fetch loop.
Effect cleanup: react runs cleanup before re-running the effect (on symbol change) and on unmount.

example.walkthrough: Effects that create persistent resources — subscriptions, timers, listeners — must return a cleanup function. Without it, each symbol change leaves the old subscription alive: duplicate updates, memory growth, and setState calls on unmounted components.

pitfalls: Common trap: subscribe must be called outside the effect because effects cannot hold subscription handles.
Common trap: use useRef for the total so updates don't trigger extra renders.
Common trap: setUser inside .then creates a promise cycle; the state setter must be called synchronously.
Common trap: the empty dependency array prevents re-renders; add count to the dependencies.

lessons.title: Routing & Data — Core concepts
concepts: React Router loaders run before the route element renders; the component reads the result with useLoaderData, and errorElement renders when the loader (or the route's render) throws. (React Router actions and the newer useActionState are alternatives, but preventDefault remains the fundamental fix.).

URL params vs search params: mixing them up is common: path params identify the resource, search params carry optional UI state like filters and sorting. A native form submission navigates the browser (GET/POST to the action URL, defaulting to the current page).

TanStack Query marks cached data stale immediately by default (staleTime: 0), so any remount triggers a background refetch. Without cancellation, a slow response for an earlier query can land after the current one and overwrite state — the classic race condition.
staleTime vs cacheTime: raising staleTime defines a freshness window during which cached data is served without refetching.

example.walkthrough: useParams extracts dynamic path segments defined in the route pattern (:id). Everything after ? is the query string, handled by useSearchParams, which returns a URLSearchParams-backed pair.

pitfalls: Common trap: useParams returns all values from the URL including query strings, so it already includes the search term.
Common trap: query strings must be stored in component state because React Router ignores everything after ?.
Common trap: set cacheTime to zero so every mount refetches, guaranteeing fresh data.
Common trap: forms in React must use uncontrolled inputs or the browser blocks submission.

lessons.title: Performance — Core concepts
concepts: useCallback: wrapping the callback in useCallback (with correct deps) gives it a stable identity.
UseMemo caches the result of an expensive computation and only recomputes when its dependencies change. Memoizing the value with useMemo (deps [theme]) keeps the reference stable.

Expensive computation: useDeferredValue splits the update: the input stays on the urgent, responsive value while the expensive list re-renders against a deferred (slightly lagging) value, and React can interrupt the background render if the user keeps typing.
Context uses reference identity: when the provider's value prop is a new object (a fresh literal each render), React notifies all consumers regardless of whether the contents changed.

example.walkthrough: React.lazy wraps a dynamic import() so the component becomes its own chunk, fetched only when first rendered; Suspense provides the loading fallback. Route-level splitting is the highest-leverage split: visitors who never open /admin never download admin code. (Named exports need an intermediate module re-exporting as default for lazy.).

pitfalls: Common trap: consumers must be wrapped in React.memo or context updates propagate to the whole tree.
Common trap: use React.memo on each row so only changed rows re-render.
Common trap: code splitting only works with class components.
Common trap: move the computation into useEffect and store the result in state to avoid blocking the render phase.

lessons.title: React Frontend — Core concepts
concepts: Components are pure-ish functions of props and state: the same inputs should render the same UI, and side effects belong in event handlers or useEffect, never in the render body.

Hooks close over the render they were created in. That is why dependency arrays matter and why the functional updater form (setState(prev => ...)) is the safe way to compute new state from old state inside callbacks.

State lives where it is used: local useState for form fields and toggles, lifted state for shared siblings, Context or a store for genuinely global data — and global state should be split by update frequency to avoid render storms.
React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback only help when prop and dependency references are stable. An inline object literal defeats memoization every time, so stabilize first, memoize second.
Keys are identity, not decoration. A stable, unique key lets the reconciler preserve component state and DOM across reorders and inserts; array indices as keys break exactly when the list changes.

Routing is just state with a URL. Route-level code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense keeps first paint fast, and data loading belongs in the route (or a loader) so navigation and fetching stay in sync.

example.walkthrough: The effect depends on userId, so it re-runs only when the user changes. The cancelled flag is the classic unmount guard: the cleanup sets it, and the promise handler checks it, so a late response never sets state on an unmounted component.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling setState during render — it schedules another render immediately and can loop; derive values directly or move the update into an effect or handler.
Common trap: an empty dependency array with values read inside the effect — the effect sees only the first render's values; list every reactive value the effect uses.
Common trap: spreading props into Context value objects inline — every render creates a new object and re-renders all consumers; memoize the value.
Common trap: optimizing before measuring — wrap in React.memo without profiling first and you add comparison cost while the real bottleneck (e.g., a huge list without virtualization) stays untouched.

simulations.title: The stale closure
simulations.brief: A counter button works on first click, then the count stops updating — the displayed value freezes while clicks keep registering.

steps.symptom: First click: 0 → 1. Later clicks: display stays 1, though the handler fires.
options: Read line 6: the effect closure captured the FIRST count value — setCount(count + 1) always computes 0 + 1
The button needs a key prop
steps.explain: The effect ran once (empty deps), so its closure froze count at 0. Every tick computes 0 + 1 — the stale closure.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: the closure captured count = 0 forever.
evidence: // deps: [] — effect never re-runs, closure never refreshes
options: Use the functional update: setCount(c => c + 1) — it reads the latest state, not the closed-over value
Add count to the deps array
steps.explain: The updater form setCount(c => c + 1) receives the current state at call time — immune to stale closures. (Adding count to deps would also work but resets the timer every tick.)

steps.symptom: Fix applied with the functional update. Verify.
options: Confirm the display increments every second without resetting the interval
steps.explain: Behavior is the proof: steady increments with one interval running means the closure bug is gone.

simulations.debrief: Effects capture the render's values forever. When an effect needs fresh state, use the functional updater — it reads current state at call time, not closure time.

simulations.title: Render and commit
simulations.brief: Restore the order of React's render-commit cycle.

steps.context: Arrange the phases in the order React executes them.
items: Render phase: compute the new element tree
Reconciliation: diff against the previous tree
Commit phase: apply DOM updates
Effects run (useEffect callbacks)
Browser paints the result

simulations.debrief: Render → reconcile → commit → effects → paint. Effects run after the DOM updates — that's why they can safely measure layout.

simulations.title: State or props?
simulations.brief: A value is needed in two sibling components. Decide where it lives.

steps.text: SearchBox and ResultsList are siblings; both need the query string. Where does query live?

choices.label: Lift it to their common parent and pass it down as props to both
choices.feedback: Right: shared state lives in the closest common ancestor — single source of truth, passed down.

choices.label: Duplicate it in each component's useState
choices.feedback: Duplicated state drifts out of sync — the classic two-sources-of-truth bug.

choices.label: Store it in a global variable outside React
choices.feedback: Globals bypass React's rendering — updates won't re-render.

steps.text: The query now also needs to survive a page reload. What changes?

choices.label: Persist it (e.g. localStorage) and hydrate the state on mount — the state still lives in React, with a persistent backing
choices.feedback: Right: lift for sharing, persist for survival. The state model doesn't change, only its backing.

choices.label: Move everything to the URL and drop the state
choices.feedback: URL state is legitimate for shareable queries, but it's a product decision, not a requirement.

choices.label: Keep it in useState and hope the user doesn't reload
choices.feedback: Hope is not a persistence strategy.

simulations.debrief: Shared state lifts to the common parent; persistence is a separate concern layered underneath. Never duplicate state to share it.

engines allows node >= 14 but the project uses React 19-era tooling that needs a modern Node.
issues.fix: Raise the engines range to match the toolchain (e.g. >= 20).

simulations.debrief: Build configs fail on spelling and on drift: a typo'd script name and an engines range that no longer matches the toolchain.

sections.heading: Components & JSX
items: Keys — Keys tell React which component instance corresponds to which data across renders. Returning arrays with keys also works but is noisier.

Controlled components — prop drilling makes intermediate components coupled to data they don't consume. An input with a value prop and no onChange is a controlled component whose displayed value is locked to state.

Form inputs — react even warns about it: 'You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler.' Adding onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} makes each keystroke flow through state back into the input.
Composition — the idiomatic fixes are composition (pass the deep content as children so Layout never sees the props) or context (provide theme/user once, consume where needed).

Effects that create persistent resources — subscriptions, timers, listeners — must return a cleanup function. Without it, each symbol change leaves the old subscription alive: duplicate updates, memory growth, and setState calls on unmounted components.

sections.heading: Performance
items: UseMemo — UseMemo caches the result of an expensive computation and only recomputes when its dependencies change. Memoizing the value with useMemo (deps [theme]) keeps the reference stable.

Expensive computation — useDeferredValue splits the update: the input stays on the urgent, responsive value while the expensive list re-renders against a deferred (slightly lagging) value, and React can interrupt the background render if the user keeps typing.
Context uses reference identity — when the provider's value prop is a new object (a fresh literal each render), React notifies all consumers regardless of whether the contents changed.
Common trap — consumers must be wrapped in React.memo or context updates propagate to the whole tree.
Common trap — use React.memo on each row so only changed rows re-render.
Common trap — code splitting only works with class components.
Common trap — move the computation into useEffect and store the result in state to avoid blocking the render phase.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Components & JSX: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one State & Effects lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Routing & Data terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
